drills.q: Compare the three Azure Functions hosting plans on scale-to-zero, cold start, VNet support, and billing.
drills.a: Consumption: scales to zero, seconds-long cold start, no VNet, pay-per-execution. Premium: no cold start (always warm), VNet native, pays even when idle. Flex Consumption: scales to zero with optional always-ready instances, native VNet, and is Microsoft's current default recommendation for new workloads.

drills.q: What two limitations of the Consumption plan does Flex Consumption specifically address?
drills.a: No VNet integration and no way to reduce cold starts short of upgrading to the always-on, always-billed Premium plan. Flex adds native VNet support and optional per-function always-ready instances while keeping Consumption's scale-to-zero economics.

drills.q: Explain mechanically what happens during a Consumption-plan cold start and name the levers that actually reduce it.
drills.a: Sandbox allocation, deployment package pull, language worker startup, and static/DI initialization all happen before the trigger handler runs -- heavy DI graphs or large packages push this past 10 seconds. Real levers: trimming package size and dependencies, avoiding synchronous startup work, a lighter runtime, or structurally moving to Flex always-ready instances or Premium.

drills.q: Distinguish a trigger from a binding, and contrast this model with how AWS Lambda handles equivalent I/O.
drills.a: A trigger is the single event invoking the function, carrying the payload. Bindings are declarative additional input/output configured alongside the trigger (fetch a document, write a queue message) requiring no SDK calls. Lambda has no equivalent declarative layer -- equivalent reads/writes require explicit SDK calls in the handler, though Lambda supports a much broader native event-source count.

drills.q: Architecturally compare Durable Functions to AWS Step Functions.
drills.a: Durable Functions is code-first: the orchestrator function's actual code is the workflow definition, executed via deterministic replay against an append-only history. Step Functions is state-machine-first: a declarative JSON/ASL document defines the workflow, with Lambda functions as task bodies invoked by defined state transitions.

drills.q: Explain the Durable Functions replay mechanism in detail, including what 'short-circuit' means here.
drills.a: Every scheduled activity call and result is persisted as an append-only history. Each time the orchestrator resumes, the framework reruns the orchestrator function from the start, but for any call already recorded in history it 'short-circuits' -- instantly returns the recorded result instead of re-executing the activity -- so only genuinely new work actually runs.

drills.q: Why is determinism a hard requirement for Durable Functions orchestrator code? Name two forbidden operations and their durable-safe replacements.
drills.a: Replay must reproduce the exact same sequence of calls as the original run to correctly match recorded history; any nondeterminism (different computed values across replays) can desync that match, causing errors or silently duplicated side effects. Forbidden: DateTime.Now/datetime.now() (use context.current_utc_datetime), and direct random generation or I/O (must go through durable-safe context APIs or activity functions).

drills.q: A team deploys a code change to a Durable Functions orchestrator while thousands of instances are in-flight. What breaks and how do you prevent it?
drills.a: In-flight instances replay against the newly deployed code; if the call sequence or branching logic changed, the instance's recorded history no longer matches the new code path, desyncing replay and causing errors or wrong behavior for that instance. Prevention: use orchestration versioning to pin in-flight instances to their original code version, or avoid changing an orchestrator's call shape and ship breaking changes as a new function/version instead.

drills.q: Design an order-fulfillment workflow needing sequential payment charge, parallel inventory reservation across N items, an optional human-approval step for high-value orders, and shipping. Which Durable Functions patterns apply, and what must accompany the approval step?
drills.a: Function chaining for the sequential payment charge; fan-out/fan-in for parallel inventory reservation waiting on all results; the human-interaction pattern (wait_for_external_event) for approval, which must be paired with a timeout (via task_any racing the event against a durable timer) or the orchestration can wait indefinitely and silently consume storage.

drills.q: A fan-out/fan-in orchestration processing 50,000 items times out. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Scheduling tens of thousands of parallel activity calls at once can overwhelm the storage/queue provider backing the Durable Task Framework and bloats the orchestration's history, slowing every replay since the whole history is walked on each resume. Fix: shard the work into sub-orchestrations handling smaller batches (e.g., 500-1000 items) rather than one massive fan-out from a single orchestrator.

drills.q: A customer-facing HTTP API on Azure Functions needs a guaranteed sub-200ms p99. What plan/configuration do you choose, and what's the honest cost tradeoff?
drills.a: Flex Consumption with always-ready instances configured for that function (paying the idle-baseline rate for guaranteed warm capacity), or Premium if VNet or consistently high load justifies its always-on cost. Pure on-demand Consumption cannot realistically guarantee this given multi-second cold-start risk; guaranteeing no cold start always means paying for some form of continuously-provisioned capacity -- there's no way to get true scale-to-zero and a hard latency SLA simultaneously.
